clinicalScope: Physical examination as a systematic bedside assessment of patients in East African and other low‑resource hospital settings
subject: Public health
summary: Physical examination is the clinician’s first, low‑cost tool to gather objective data about a patient’s health. In East African hospitals it guides diagnosis, triage and public‑health surveillance when laboratory tests are limited.

sections.p: Physical examination is a structured, hands‑on assessment of the body that converts visual, tactile and auditory cues into clinical information. In low‑resource settings it also serves as a surveillance instrument for common community diseases.
b: Systematic sequence: general appearance → vital signs → focused organ systems
Combines inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
Provides immediate data for triage, diagnosis and public‑health reporting
Adaptable to bedside, ward, or community outreach

sections.p: In sub‑Saharan Africa, limited laboratory capacity means that up to 70 % of initial diagnoses rely on bedside findings, influencing outcomes for malaria, TB, HIV‑related opportunistic infections and non‑communicable diseases.
b: High burden of febrile illnesses where fever pattern and organomegaly guide treatment
Cardiovascular disease rising; pulse, blood pressure and peripheral signs remain core
Maternal mortality linked to missed signs of pre‑eclampsia (e.g., edema, reflexes)
Childhood malnutrition identified by skin turgor, muscle wasting, and growth charts

sections.p: The quality of a physical exam depends on clinician training, patient cooperation, and environmental factors such as lighting and privacy.
b: Limited training → missed subtle signs (e.g., early meningismus)
Cultural norms may restrict exposure of certain body parts
Crowded wards reduce time per patient, increasing error risk
Availability of basic tools (stethoscope, sphygmomanometer) is essential

sections.p: Aggregated exam findings feed into disease‑surveillance systems (e.g., Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response, IDSR).
b: Cluster of fever + splenomegaly → suspect malaria outbreak
Sudden rise in jaundice + hepatomegaly → possible hepatitis A epidemic
Increased prevalence of peripheral edema → monitor for heart failure surge
Standardised forms (WHO STEPwise) ensure comparable data

sections.p: Physical signs are used for opportunistic screening during routine visits.
b: Blood pressure measurement for hypertension screening
BMI and waist circumference for metabolic risk
Oral inspection for tobacco‑related lesions
Neurological exam for early HIV neuropathy

sections.p: When a sign suggests a treatable condition, immediate bedside interventions can be lifesaving.
b: Detecting a rapid, weak pulse → initiate fluid bolus for shock
Identifying neck stiffness → start empiric meningitis therapy
Finding cyanosis → give supplemental oxygen and assess airway
Spotting severe pallor → order urgent hemoglobin test and consider transfusion

sections.p: National guidelines (e.g., Kenya Clinical Guidelines) embed physical exam steps into standard operating procedures for triage and referral.
b: Task‑shifting: nurses trained to perform basic exam and trigger physician review
Audit tools track exam completeness and correlate with outcomes
Supply chains prioritize basic equipment (BP cuffs, stethoscopes)
Policy encourages documentation for health‑information systems

sections.p: A well‑performed exam reduces diagnostic delays for marginalized groups.
b: Mobile clinics use portable exam kits to reach remote villages
Community health workers trained in simple signs (e.g., edema) refer early
Gender‑sensitive approaches improve acceptance of abdominal exams
Language‑appropriate education links exam findings to self‑care

sections.p: Quality of physical examination is monitored through direct observation, checklists, and patient outcomes.
b: Mini‑CEX (clinical evaluation exercise) scores for exam technique
Audit of missed diagnoses vs. documented exam findings
Patient satisfaction surveys on thoroughness of exam
Feedback loops to training programs

sections.p: Physical examination remains the cornerstone for bedside reasoning, especially when imaging or labs are unavailable.
b: Differentiates malaria from bacterial sepsis by pattern of fever and splenomegaly
Distinguishes heart failure from severe anemia via jugular venous pressure and capillary refill
Identifies meningitis through Kernig/Brudzinski signs when lumbar puncture is delayed
Guides HIV opportunistic infection work‑up through oral thrush, lymphadenopathy, and skin lesions

sections.p: Reliance on exam alone can miss early disease or mimic other conditions.
b: Subtle early TB may lack palpable lymph nodes
Obesity masks heart sounds, leading to missed murmurs
Cultural modesty may limit chest auscultation
Inter‑observer variability without standardised training

sections.p: A reproducible, step‑wise approach maximises data capture and reduces omissions.
b: 1. General: level of consciousness, distress, nutrition, skin colour
2. Vital signs: BP, pulse, RR, temperature, SpO₂
3. Head & neck: eyes (pupils), ears, oral cavity, lymph nodes
4. Cardiovascular: palpate apex beat, auscultate heart sounds, assess JVP
5. Respiratory: inspect chest rise, palpate tactile fremitus, percuss, auscultate breath sounds
6. Abdomen: inspect, auscultate bowel sounds, palpate liver, spleen, tenderness
7. Extremities: edema, pulses, skin temperature, neurological checks

sections.p: When a listed test is unavailable, use the next best clinical proxy (e.g., capillary refill for perfusion when pulse oximeter is absent).

t.b: Is the patient hypertensive? → ≥140/90 mmHg indicates hypertension, prompting lifestyle advice and possible pharmacotherapy
Is oxygenation adequate? → SpO₂ <90 % signals hypoxaemia, requiring supplemental O₂
Are there abnormal sounds? → New murmur suggests valvular disease; absent S1 may indicate severe cardiomyopathy
Is the liver enlarged? → Palpable edge >2 cm below costal margin suggests hepatomegaly, common in malaria or hepatitis
Is consciousness impaired? → GCS ≤8 mandates airway protection

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained sudden collapse or loss of consciousness
Rapidly rising fever with neck stiffness

faq.q: Can a physical exam replace laboratory tests?
faq.a: It can guide immediate decisions but should be complemented by labs when available.

faq.q: What if I lack a stethoscope?
faq.a: Use a simple plastic tubing to amplify breath sounds; focus on visual and tactile cues.

faq.q: How often should vital signs be re‑checked?
faq.a: At least every 30 minutes for unstable patients and every 4–6 hours for stable admissions.

exam: How would you differentiate malaria from bacterial sepsis using only bedside findings? — Look for periodic fever, splenomegaly, and relative bradycardia in malaria versus continuous high fever, hypotension, and warm extremities in sepsis.

A patient presents with jaundice, mild right‑upper‑quadrant tenderness, and a normal bilirubin level on bedside test. What is your next step? — Consider hepatitis or hemolysis; obtain a point‑of‑care bilirubin if possible, otherwise arrange referral for laboratory confirmation.

During triage you note a pulse of 110 bpm, capillary refill >3 seconds, and cool extremities. What does this indicate and what immediate action is required? — Signs of compensated shock; start rapid IV crystalloid bolus and monitor vitals.

What physical sign distinguishes pericardial tamponade from severe asthma in a patient with dyspnoea? — Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg drop in systolic BP on inspiration) suggests tamponade; absent in asthma.
Explain why a low‑tech JVP assessment is valuable in a setting without echocardiography. — Elevated JVP indicates right‑sided heart failure or volume overload, guiding diuretic therapy.

A child with cough has wheeze only on expiration and a normal chest exam between attacks. How does this affect your diagnosis? — Suggests intermittent asthma; treat with bronchodilator trial and educate on trigger avoidance.

You encounter a patient with pallor, tachycardia, and a systolic murmur. What are the possible diagnoses and how would you prioritize investigations? — Consider severe anemia vs. congenital heart disease; prioritize hemoglobin point‑of‑care test, then echocardiography if anemia excluded.

During a community health visit you find several adults with peripheral edema and hypertension. What public‑health intervention should be initiated? — Screen for chronic kidney disease and heart failure; start low‑salt diet education and arrange BP control programs.

How does cultural modesty affect the physical exam and what strategies mitigate missed findings? — May limit chest/abdominal exposure; use gender‑matched examiners, explain purpose, and obtain consent to ensure completeness.

What are the key components of a documented physical exam for inclusion in the national surveillance database? — Date/time, patient identifiers, vital signs, general appearance, organ‑specific findings, and any abnormal signs with severity grading.
